headline: Halfway Rock on the push: cod hold steady, bass slide into the dark tide
subhead: With the moon rounding to full, Casco Bay's current is sharpening — and the bite is moving toward the edges of light.
body_markdown:
Stood on the rail off Halfway Rock this week and watched the tide line stack up harder than it has all month — a clean seam of green water pushing against the darker water off the ledge, gulls working it tight. That's the tell. The moon rounds to full tomorrow night, and the current through the bay's ledges and channels has been building toward it for days. We flagged this pattern last week, that the push toward full moon would strengthen the current enough to concentrate bait against structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now from Halfway Rock down through the Harpswell ledges.

The broader picture for Casco Bay right now is a stable one, and stable is the right word for late August here. While water farther south sits in that thermally stressed, structure-and-night-bite holding pattern for striped bass, the Gulf of Maine's cooler water keeps our fishery on a more even keel. It's not blazing, but it's dependable — the kind of program where a careful angler who reads the tide correctly will out-fish someone running blind on a schedule that doesn't match the current.

Striped bass are in exactly the kind of late-summer lull you'd expect this time of year, but they haven't gone anywhere — they've just shifted their address to the structure and to the low-light hours. Daytime fish are holding tight to the ledges off Bailey Island and along the drop-offs on the west side of Peaks Island, sitting deep against rock in 20 to 35 feet through the heat of the day and sliding up onto the flats and eddies as the light fails. The evening flood tide, roughly two hours before and after the top, has been the most consistent window — bass working the current seams off Cape Small and around the back side of Halfway Rock on tube-and-worm rigs fished slow along bottom, or live mackerel drifted on a fish-finder rig where the ledge drops into deeper water. Sluggos in bone or bunker colors, worked slow on a jighead after dark near the Two Lights ledges, have also been drawing strikes from fish that won't touch anything moving fast in daylight.

Bluefish are mixing into that same program in patches — nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around, but cocktail-sized blues have been showing up on the troll and on bucktails intended for bass, particularly on the outgoing tide off Peaks Island and in the deeper water south of Halfway Rock. Worth keeping a wire leader rigged as insurance if you're throwing plugs in that zone right now.

Groundfish have been the more reliable story this week. Cod and pollock are holding on the deep ledges around Halfway Rock and off Bailey Island, typically in 80 to 120 feet, and the bite has been most productive on the slack around the tide change — not the dead slack itself, but the twenty minutes on either side when the current eases enough to hold bottom without three ounces of extra lead. Diamond jigs in the 4- to 6-ounce range, tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly, have been the go-to presentation, worked in a slow lift-and-drop just off bottom. Haddock have been mixed in on some of the deeper structure toward Cape Small, though they're spottier than the cod right now — worth a few drifts but not a spot to build a whole day around yet.

Mackerel, which usually make their loudest push through the bay back in May, have thinned out but haven't disappeared. Small schools are still showing around the Peaks Island wharf pilings and along the edges near Halfway Rock, enough to fill a bait bucket on a Sabiki rig if you catch them working the surface early in the morning before the wind picks up. That live mackerel is worth more to a bass angler than almost anything in the tackle box right now — a lively mackerel free-lined or fished on a fish-finder rig near ledge structure at dusk has been the most consistent producer of the bigger bass reported this week.

Looking ahead, the building tide toward tomorrow's full moon should sharpen these bite windows rather than blow them out. Bigger swings mean stronger current at structure like Halfway Rock and the Harpswell ledges, which typically means better bait concentration and a tighter window when the fish commit. If the wind stays out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 range as it has, expect the pattern to hold through the weekend — work the evening flood at the ledges for bass, hit the slack tide change on the deep structure for cod, and don't overlook an early-morning pass with the Sabiki rig before the mackerel schools scatter with the sun. The bigger question worth watching into September is whether this warm pulse in Maine's coastal water continues to hold or starts to retreat as nights cool — that shift, when it comes, will be the signal that the real fall program is starting rather than this holding pattern we're in now.
